metadata.title: Interpretable machine learning reveals key determinants of creative thinking among East Asian students: Evidence from PISA 2022

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for creative thinking and constructs a student-level creative thinking composite score from 10 plausible values combined using Rubin’s rules, explicitly stating that this pooling reflects PISA’s complex survey design. The manuscript does not report the use of explicit student/sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight procedures, so it is unclear whether complex-survey weighting was applied directly in the ML training stage. Because the models are trained in Python with scikit-learn/XGBoost/LightGBM, the paper’s weighting strategy appears to rely on the PV construction rather than explicitly incorporating survey weights into the learners. Analysts should therefore treat the results as conditional on the PV-based scoring approach and note that economy-level clustering was addressed via Leave-One-Group-Out cross-validation rather than via weight-based variance estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses PISA 2022 data for East Asian economies that participated in the creative thinking computer-based assessment module. Japan was excluded because it did not participate in the creative thinking assessment. The dependent variable (creative thinking) is based on human-rated open-ended tasks across three cognitive facets, scaled to a 0–60 composite using 10 plausible values. Predictor variables were restricted to a set of 30 variables; variables with missing-data rates exceeding 10% were excluded. Missing values in the remaining predictors were imputed using k-nearest neighbors (KNNImputer) within each training fold of the nested resampling procedure to prevent data leakage.

confounders_identified.variable_name: ICT for school activities outside class

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (East Asian economies; student-level composite 0–60)
main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking score (PVs combined via Rubin’s rules)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison (100 random 80/20 splits with 5-fold CV tuning): LightGBM R²=0.6304 (SD=0.0078), RMSE=6.24 (SD=0.06), MAE=4.96 (SD=0.05). Robustness (LOGO-CV holding out each economy): ENR R²=0.4440 (±0.1011) vs LightGBM R²=0.3898 (±0.1126); paired t-test t=2.8040, p=0.0486.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking data for Hong Kong (China), Macau (China), Chinese Taipei, South Korea, and Singapore, the study leveraged reading performance, science performance, family ESCS, math performance, and gender to predict students’ creative thinking scores, finding that LightGBM achieved the highest overall predictive fit (R²≈0.63; RMSE≈6.24; MAE≈4.96) and that reading performance was the most influential predictor. This indicates that strengthening reading-related competencies and supporting students’ academic foundations alongside socioeconomic and gender-sensitive supports may be promising for improving creative thinking, while the SHAP-based importance is predictive (not causal) and generalizability across economies is moderated by the LOGO-CV robustness results.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 creative thinking (computer-based open-ended tasks) for five East Asian economies—Hong Kong (China), Macau (China), Chinese Taipei, South Korea, and Singapore—excluding Japan due to non-participation in the creative thinking module. Creative thinking is scaled to a 0–60 composite using 10 plausible values, pooled with Rubin’s rules, and modeled with five interpretable ML regressors (Elastic Net, SVR, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM). Across 100 repeated 80/20 train-test splits (with nested preprocessing and 5-fold CV hyperparameter tuning), LightGBM performed best with R²=0.6304 (SD=0.0078), RMSE=6.24 (SD=0.06), and MAE=4.96 (SD=0.05). SHAP interpretation shows reading performance as the top predictor, followed by science performance, ESCS, math performance, and gender. A LOGO-CV robustness check (holding out each economy) reduced LightGBM’s advantage and even favored ENR, and the authors’ SHAP explanations reflect predictive associations rather than causal effects.
